Their line began at Heleph and the oak at Zaanannim, passed Adami-nekeb and Jabneel, and went on to Lakkum. The Jordan was its end.
It turned west to Aznoth-tabor and ran from there to Hukkok. Zebulun lay on its south, Asher on its west, and Judah{l} at the Jordan on its east.
The walled towns were Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, Chinnereth,
Adamah, Ramah, Hazor,
Kedesh, Edrei, and En-hazor,
along with Yiron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath, and Beth-shemesh. Together there were nineteen towns, each with villages.
These towns and villages were the share of the tribe of Naphtali, by clan.
The seventh lot came out for the tribe of Dan,{m} for its clans.
Their land took in Zorah, Eshtaol, Ir-shemesh,
Shaalabbin, Aijalon, Ithlah,
Elon, Timnah, Ekron,
Eltekeh, Gibbethon, Baalath,
Jehud, Bene-berak, Gath-rimmon,
Me-jarkon, and Rakkon, with the land facing Joppa.

Later the Danites lost their land.{n} They went up, attacked Leshem, captured it, and killed its people with the sword. They moved in and settled there. They renamed Leshem “Dan,” after their ancestor Dan.
These towns and villages were the share of the tribe of Dan, by clan.
When the Israelites had finished dividing the land, they gave Joshua son of Nun a share among them.
Yahweh had given an order, so they gave him the town he had asked for. It was Timnath-serah{o}, in Ephraim’s hills. Joshua built it up again and made his home there.

These are the shares that Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the family heads of the tribes handed out by lot at Shiloh, in front of Yahweh, at the entrance to the meeting tent. That is how they finished dividing the land.

notes.text: Simeon means “heard” (Genesis 29:33).
Or “Shema,” as in 15:26 and 1 Chronicles 4:28. The list adds up to thirteen only if Sheba repeats Beersheba.
Zebulun may mean “honor” or “dwelling” (Genesis 30:20).
This is a Bethlehem in Galilee, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) northwest of Nazareth, not Bethlehem of Judah.
Issachar sounds like the Hebrew for “there is a reward” (Genesis 30:18).
Asher means “happy” or “blessed” (Genesis 30:13).
Carmel means “garden land” or “orchard.”
Some Hebrew manuscripts read Abdon (compare 21:30).
Tyre (Hebrew Tsor) means “rock.”
Hebrew “from Hebel.” The reading Mahalab, a town known from Assyrian records, takes a small change.
Naphtali means “my wrestling” (Genesis 30:8).
That is how the Hebrew reads. The Greek Old Testament lacks “and Judah.” The phrase may refer to Jair’s towns east of the Jordan (1 Chronicles 2:21-23), or the text may be damaged.
Dan means “he judged” or “judge” (Genesis 30:6).

Literally “went out from them.” The Greek Old Testament has a different text in verses 47-48. It says the Amorites pushed the Danites into the hill country and would not let them come down to the plain, that the Danites took Lachish (the Hebrew has Leshem) and named it Lasendan, and that the Amorites stayed in Edom and Shaalbim until Ephraim made them pay tribute. Compare Judges 1:34-35; 18:27-29.

Timnath-serah means “portion that remains” (or “extra portion”). Judges 2:9 calls it Timnath-heres, “portion of the sun,” and Serah may be a deliberate reversal of the letters. The Greek Old Testament spells it Thamnasarach.

verses.text: Then Yahweh said to Joshua,
“Tell the people of Israel to pick the towns of safety. I described them to you through Moses.
A person who kills someone by accident, without meaning to, can run to one of them. In these towns you will be safe from the family avenger.{a}
The killer must flee to one of these towns, stop at the gate, and tell the town’s elders his story. They must bring him inside, give him a home, and let him stay with them.{b}
If the family avenger comes after him, the people must not hand the killer over. He killed his neighbor by accident and had no earlier hatred for him.
He must stay there until the assembly has judged his case, and until the high priest of that time has died. After that, the killer may return to the home in the town he ran from.”
So they set apart Kedesh{c} in Galilee,{d} in Naphtali’s hills, Shechem{e} in Ephraim’s hills, and Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in Judah’s hills.
On the other side of the Jordan, across from Jericho, they chose Bezer on the desert plateau, from Reuben’s land, Ramoth in Gilead, from Gad’s land, and Golan in Bashan, from Manasseh’s land.

These towns were meant for every Israelite and for the foreigners living among them. Anyone who killed by accident could flee there. The family avenger could not kill him before he stood trial in front of the community.

notes.text: Hebrew go’el haddam, the nearest relative, whose duty was to take responsibility when a family member was killed. The same word go’el means “redeemer” in other places (Ruth 4:1-6).

The Greek Old Testament lacks verses 4-6 and the phrase “without knowing it” in verse 3. In verse 3 it reads instead, “until he stands before the community for judgment.” The longer Hebrew text echoes Deuteronomy 19:1-13, and the shorter Greek text echoes Numbers 35:9-28.
Kedesh means “holy place.”
Galilee (Hebrew galil) means “circle” or “district.”
Shechem means “shoulder” or “ridge,” perhaps from its place on the saddle between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim.

verses.text: The Levites’ family heads stepped forward. Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the leaders of the other tribes’ families were waiting.
At Shiloh, in the land of Canaan, they spoke up. “Yahweh gave a command through Moses,” they said. “He told you to give us towns for living in, with pastures for our livestock.”
So the Israelites obeyed Yahweh’s order and gave the Levites these towns and pastures out of their own land.
The first lot came out for the Kohathite clans. The Levites descended from Aaron the priest received thirteen towns by lot from the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin.
The other Kohathites received ten towns by lot from the clans of Ephraim, from Dan, and from half of Manasseh.
The Gershonites received thirteen towns by lot from the clans of Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and the half-tribe of Manasseh in Bashan.
The Merarites, by clan, received twelve towns from Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun.
By lot, the Israelites gave the Levites these towns and their pastures, as Yahweh had ordered through Moses.
From the tribes of Judah and Simeon they gave the towns named here.
They went to the descendants of Aaron from the Kohathite clans of Levi, because theirs was the first lot.
They gave them Kiriath-arba (Arba was Anak’s father), which is Hebron, in the hill country of Judah, together with the pastures around it.
But the fields and villages belonging to the town had been given to Caleb son of Jephunneh as his own.
To the descendants of Aaron the priest they gave Hebron, a town of safety for killers, with its pastures, and also Libnah with its pastures,
Jattir and Eshtemoa with their pastures,
Holon and Debir with their pastures,
Ain,{a} Juttah, and Beth-shemesh, each with its pastures. These two tribes gave nine towns.
From the tribe of Benjamin they gave Gibeon and Geba with their pastures,
and Anathoth{b} and Almon with their pastures. That made four towns.
The priests, Aaron’s descendants, received thirteen towns in all, with their pastures.
The remaining Kohathite clans of the Levites were given towns from the tribe of Ephraim.
They received Shechem, a town of safety for killers, in the hill country of Ephraim, with its pastures, and also Gezer with its pastures,
Kibzaim and Beth-horon with their pastures. That made four towns.
From the tribe of Dan they received Elteke and Gibbethon,
then Aijalon and Gath-rimmon, each with its pastures. That made four towns.
Half of Manasseh’s tribe gave them Taanach and Gath-rimmon,{c} each with its pastures. That made two towns.
So the remaining Kohathite clans received ten towns with their pastures.
The Gershonite clans of the Levites received two towns from half of Manasseh’s tribe: Golan in Bashan, a town of safety for killers, and Be-eshterah,{d} each with its pastures.
Issachar gave them Kishion and Daberath,
then Jarmuth and En-gannim, each with its pastures. That made four towns.
Asher gave them Mishal and Abdon,
then Helkath and Rehob, each with its pastures. That made four towns.
Naphtali gave them Kedesh in Galilee, a town of safety for killers, plus Hammoth-dor and Kartan, each with its pastures. That made three towns.
All told, the Gershonite clans received thirteen towns with their pastures.
The last of the Levites, the Merarite clans, received towns too. Zebulun gave Jokneam and Kartah,
then Dimnah and Nahalal, each with its pastures. That made four towns.
Reuben{e} gave Bezer and Jahaz,
then Kedemoth and Mephaath, each with its pastures. That made four towns.
Gad gave Ramoth in Gilead, a town of safety for killers, and Mahanaim,
then Heshbon and Jazer, each with its pastures. That made four towns in all.
The Merarite clans, the last of the Levite families, were given twelve towns in all.
In all, the Levites held forty-eight towns, with their pastures, inside the land of the Israelites.
Every one of these towns had pastureland around it.{f}
So Yahweh gave Israel all the land he had promised with an oath to their ancestors. They took it and settled in it.
On every side Yahweh gave them peace, just as he had sworn to their ancestors. No enemy could stand up to them, for Yahweh put every enemy in their power.
Of all the good promises Yahweh made to Israel’s people, not one was left unkept. Every one came true.

notes.text: Ain means “spring.” The Greek Old Testament and 1 Chronicles 6:59 read Ashan.
Anathoth was later the hometown of the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:1).
Repeating Gath-rimmon from verse 24 is probably a copying mistake. 1 Chronicles 6:70 has Bileam (that is, Ibleam), and the Greek Old Testament reads Iebatha.
Be-eshterah is probably a short form of Beth-ashtarah, “house of Astarte.” 1 Chronicles 6:71 has Ashtaroth.

Many Hebrew manuscripts and some printed editions of the Hebrew Bible lack verses 36-37, though the text followed here has them. They are in the Greek Old Testament and in 1 Chronicles 6:78-79, and the totals in verses 7 and 40 (twelve towns) need them.

The Greek Old Testament adds, “Joshua finished dividing the land by its borders. The Israelites gave Joshua a share by the Lord’s command. They gave him the town he asked for, Thamnasachar in the hill country of Ephraim. Joshua built the town and lived in it. Then Joshua took the flint knives he had used to circumcise the Israelites born in the wilderness on the way, and put them in Thamnasachar.” Compare 19:49-50 and 24:31 (Greek Old Testament).

verses.text: Joshua now called for the Reubenites, the Gadites, and Manasseh’s eastern half.
“You have done all that Moses, Yahweh’s servant, ordered,” he told them. “And you have listened to me every time I gave an order.
For a long time, right up to today, you have not left your brothers. You have kept the duty Yahweh your God gave you.
Now Yahweh your God has given your brothers rest, as he promised. So go back to your tents, to the land that is yours. Moses, Yahweh’s servant, gave it to you east of the Jordan.

Only be very careful to keep the command and the teaching that Moses, Yahweh’s servant, handed down. Love Yahweh your God. Walk his whole road. Obey his commands. Hold on to him. Give him every bit of your heart and soul in service.”
With a blessing, Joshua let them go, and they returned to their tents.

Moses had given Bashan to one half of Manasseh’s tribe. To the other half, Joshua gave a place beside their brothers on the west bank of the Jordan. Joshua blessed these men too, and as he sent them home to their tents,
he said, “Go back to your tents with great riches. Take huge herds, silver, gold, bronze, iron, and piles of clothing. Share the goods you took from your enemies with your brothers.”
So the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh left the Israelites at Shiloh in Canaan. They headed home to Gilead, the land that was theirs by Yahweh’s order through Moses.
They came to the region{a} by the Jordan, still in Canaan. There the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh built an altar beside the river. It was a huge, impressive altar.
Then people told the Israelites, “Look! The tribes of Reuben and Gad and half of Manasseh have set up an altar at Canaan’s edge, in the Jordan region, facing Israel.”
When the Israelites heard it, their whole community gathered at Shiloh to march out and fight them.
But first the Israelites chose Phinehas,{b} the son of Eleazar the priest, and sent him to Reuben, Gad, and the half of Manasseh living in Gilead.
Ten leaders went with him, one for each tribe of Israel. Each one headed a family in his tribe’s clans.{c}
They came to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead and said,
“All of Yahweh’s people ask you: Why have you been unfaithful to the God of Israel? Today you have turned away from Yahweh. You built yourselves an altar and rose up against him!
Was the sin at Peor{d} not bad enough? We are still not clean from it, though a plague hit Yahweh’s people.
And now you are turning from Yahweh too! Rebel against him today, and tomorrow his anger will fall on every Israelite.

If you think the land you hold is unclean, cross over to Yahweh’s land, where his dwelling stands, and live among us. But do not rebel against Yahweh, and do not make us rebels, by building an altar of your own beside the altar of Yahweh our God.
Think of Achan son of Zerah. He broke the ban on what was set apart for destruction, and anger fell on all Israel. Others died too, not only Achan, because of his sin.”
Then the men of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh gave their answer to the heads of Israel’s families.
“The Mighty One, God, Yahweh! The Mighty One, God, Yahweh!{e} He knows, and may Israel know too! If we rebelled or betrayed Yahweh, do not spare us today.
If we built this altar to leave Yahweh, or to burn offerings on it, whether burnt, grain, or peace offerings, then let Yahweh himself punish us.
No! We were afraid. We worried that one day your children would ask ours, ‘Why should you bother with Yahweh, the God of Israel?
Yahweh set the Jordan as a border between your people and ours. Reuben and Gad, you have no share in Yahweh.’ Then your children might cause ours to stop fearing Yahweh.
That is why we decided to build an altar. We did not plan to burn offerings or make sacrifices on it.

It will be a witness between you and us, and between the children who come after us. It will show that we do serve Yahweh in his presence with our burnt offerings, sacrifices, and peace offerings. Then your children could never tell ours later, “You have no share in Yahweh.”’

We also thought, ‘Suppose people say this to us or our children someday. Then we will answer, “Look at the copy of Yahweh’s altar that our ancestors built. It was never meant for burnt offerings or sacrifices. It stands as a witness between us and you.”’

We would never rebel against Yahweh or turn away from him today by building an altar for burnt offerings, grain offerings, or sacrifices, besides the altar of Yahweh our God that stands in front of his dwelling!”
The priest Phinehas and the community leaders with him, the heads of Israel’s families, heard what the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the Manassites said. They were pleased.
Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest said, “At last we know that Yahweh lives among us. You did not turn on him in this matter. You have kept Israel from Yahweh’s hand.”
So Phinehas, Eleazar’s son the priest, and the leaders left Gilead and the men of Reuben and Gad. They went back to Canaan and gave the Israelites their report.
The Israelites were glad to hear it, and they praised God. They never spoke again of marching out to destroy the land where the Reubenites and the Gadites lived.
The Reubenites and the Gadites named the altar Witness,{f} for they said, “It is a witness between us that Yahweh is God.”

notes.text: Hebrew gelilot, “circles” or “districts,” possibly a place name, Geliloth. The same word is used in verse 11. The Greek Old Testament reads “Galaad” (Gilead).
Phinehas is an Egyptian name, probably meaning “the Nubian” (Numbers 25:7).
Hebrew “thousands,” a word for clan divisions. The same word is used in verses 21 and 30.
See Numbers 25:1-9.
Hebrew El Elohim Yahweh, three names for God, repeated as a solemn oath.

Hebrew ‘ed, “witness.” The name is not in the usual Hebrew text, which reads, “called the altar, ‘For it is a witness...’” Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac supply it. The Greek Old Testament reads, “Joshua gave a name to the altar... and said, ‘It is a witness among them.’”

subheads.1: Joshua Sends the Eastern Tribes Home

verses.text: A long time passed. Yahweh had given Israel rest from the enemies around them, and Joshua was now very old.
He called all Israel together, with its elders, heads, judges, and officers. He told them, “I am old, and my years are nearly done.
You have seen everything Yahweh your God did to these nations for you. Yahweh your God was the one who fought for you.
Listen. I have given you the nations that are left as land for your tribes. I have also given you the nations I wiped out, from the Jordan west to the Great Sea.
Yahweh your God will shove them out and drive them off as you move forward. Their land will be yours, as Yahweh your God promised.
So be strong. Keep and obey everything written in the book of the teaching of Moses. Never turn aside, whether right or left.
Do not mix with the nations still among you. Do not speak the names of their gods, swear by them, serve them, or bow to them.
Hold tight to Yahweh your God, as you have done until now.
Yahweh has driven great and strong nations out of your way. Until today nobody has beaten you.
One of you can make a thousand run away, because Yahweh your God fights on your side, just as he promised.
So take great care to love Yahweh your God.
If you turn away and cling to what is left of these nations, or if you marry their people and mingle with them,

Then be sure of this: Yahweh your God will stop driving these nations out ahead of you. They will turn into traps and snares. They will lash your backs like whips and stab your eyes like thorns, until you have vanished from this good land Yahweh your God gave you.
“Soon I will go the way everyone on earth must go. You know deep inside that not one of the good things Yahweh your God promised you has failed. All of it came true for you. Not one promise failed.
But every good thing Yahweh promised has come to you. In the same way, Yahweh will bring every bad thing on you, until he has wiped you out of this good land he gave you.

This will happen if you break the covenant Yahweh your God commanded, serve other gods, and bow down to them. Then Yahweh’s anger will blaze up, and you will soon be gone from the good land he gave you.”{a}

notes.text: The Greek Old Testament lacks the last sentence of this verse (“Yahweh’s anger will blaze...”).

verses.text: Joshua called every tribe of Israel to Shechem.{a} He summoned the elders, heads, judges, and officers of Israel, and they took their places in front of God.

Then Joshua spoke to all the people. “Yahweh, the God of Israel, says this,” he began. “‘A long time ago your ancestors lived across the River.{b} They served other gods. One of them was Terah, who had two sons, Abraham and Nahor.
Then I brought Abraham, your ancestor, from across the River. I walked him through all of Canaan and gave him a large family. Isaac was his son.
To Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau. Esau received the hills of Seir as his own land, while Jacob and his sons went down into Egypt.
After that I sent Moses and Aaron, and I struck Egypt with the troubles I brought there. And so you came out.{c}
Your ancestors came out of Egypt and reached the sea. Egyptian chariots and horsemen chased them all the way to the Red Sea.

Your ancestors cried out to Yahweh. He set a wall of darkness between you and Egypt’s army, and he pulled the sea over the Egyptians until it buried them. You watched what I did to Egypt. After that you spent a long time in the wilderness.
I brought you to the Amorites’ land, east of the Jordan. They attacked you, but I put them in your hands. You took over their land, and I destroyed them as you came.
Next, Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, prepared to attack Israel. He sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor, asking him to curse you.
I refused to listen to Balaam. Instead he blessed you again and again, and I kept you safe from him.

When you passed over the Jordan and reached Jericho, the lords{d} of that town fought you. So did the Amorites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hittites, Girgashites, Hivites, and Jebusites. Yet I put each of them in your hands.
I sent the hornet{e} ahead of you. It chased out the two Amorite kings{f} for you. Neither sword nor bow won that fight.
I handed you a country you never plowed and towns you never built, and you live in them today. You eat grapes and olives from trees you never planted.’
“Now, then, honor Yahweh. Serve him honestly and faithfully. Get rid of the gods that your ancestors worshiped east of the River and in Egypt, and serve Yahweh alone.

Maybe you think it is wrong to serve Yahweh. Then choose this very day who you will serve. Will it be the gods your ancestors had across the River? Or will it be the gods of the Amorites, whose country you now live in? My family and I will serve Yahweh.”
The people replied, “Never! We will not leave Yahweh to serve other gods!
Yahweh is our God. He rescued us and our ancestors from slavery in Egypt. He performed those mighty signs while we watched. All along our travels, and among every people we passed, he protected us.
Yahweh pushed out every nation ahead of us, even the Amorites who held this land. We will serve Yahweh as well, for he is our God.”
Joshua answered them, “You are not able to serve Yahweh. He is holy. He is a God who guards what is his. He will not pardon your rebellion or your sins.
Suppose you abandon Yahweh and follow foreign gods. He will then turn on you, bring disaster, and destroy you, though he once treated you well.”
But the people said again, “No! We will serve Yahweh.”
Joshua replied, “You are your own witnesses. You have picked Yahweh and promised to serve him.” “Yes, we are witnesses,” they said.
“Then throw out the foreign gods you have,” he said. “Give your hearts to Yahweh, the God of Israel.”
The people said, “Yahweh our God is the one we will serve. His voice is the one we will obey.”
On that day Joshua made a covenant with the people. There at Shechem{g} he set out rules and laws for them.
Joshua recorded these words in the Book of the Teaching of God. Then he picked up a large stone and stood it beneath the oak{h} beside Yahweh’s holy place.
“Look at this stone,” he told everyone. “It has heard all that Yahweh told us. If you ever lie to your God, it will speak against you.”
Then Joshua dismissed the people, and each person went to his own share of land.
Some time later Joshua son of Nun, the servant of Yahweh, died. He was 110 years old.{i}
His people buried him in the land that was his, at Timnath-serah in Ephraim’s hills, north of Mount Gaash.{j}
All through Joshua’s life, Israel served Yahweh. They kept on serving him through the lives of the elders who lived on after Joshua and had seen everything Yahweh did for Israel.{k}

Joseph’s bones had been brought up from Egypt by the Israelites. They laid them to rest at Shechem, in the field Jacob had bought for a hundred pieces of money.{l} He bought it from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father. That field became Joseph’s family’s land.
Eleazar son of Aaron died as well. His people buried him at Gibeah,{m} a hill town that belonged to his son Phinehas and lay in Ephraim’s hills.{n}

notes.text: The Greek Old Testament reads Shiloh here and in verse 25. Shechem was the place of Abraham’s first altar in the land (Genesis 12:6-7) and of Jacob’s burial of foreign gods (Genesis 35:4).
That is, the Euphrates. The same is meant in verses 3, 14, and 15.
The Greek Old Testament has a shorter text in verses 5-7. It lacks “I sent Moses and Aaron” and some other phrases.
Hebrew ba’ale, “the lords” or “citizens.”
Or “panic” or “terror” (Hebrew tsir’ah). Compare Exodus 23:28 and Deuteronomy 7:20.
The Greek Old Testament reads “twelve kings of the Amorites.” The Hebrew “two kings” means Sihon and Og (2:10).
The Greek Old Testament reads “at Shiloh, in front of the tent of the God of Israel.”
Or “terebinth,” a large tree. Compare Genesis 35:4, where Jacob hid foreign gods under the oak near Shechem.
An age of 110 years was seen as the ideal life span in Egypt. Joseph died at the same age (Genesis 50:26).
Gaash may mean “quaking” or “shaking.”

The Greek Old Testament places this verse before Joshua’s death (as verse 29). After the burial it adds that the flint knives Joshua used to circumcise the Israelites at Gilgal, after he led them out of Egypt, were laid beside him in his grave, as the Lord had commanded, and that they are still there today. Compare the Greek Old Testament addition at 21:42.

Hebrew “for a hundred qesitah,” a unit of uncertain value, perhaps a weight of silver. It appears elsewhere only in Genesis 33:19 and Job 42:11. The Greek Old Testament reads “for a hundred ewe-lambs.” Compare Genesis 33:19; Acts 7:16.
Gibeah means “hill.” The Greek Old Testament reads Gabaar.

The Greek Old Testament adds a longer ending: “On that day the Israelites took the ark of God and carried it around among them. Phinehas served as priest in place of his father Eleazar until he died, and he was buried in his own place, Gabaar. The Israelites went away, each to his own place and his own town. Then the Israelites worshiped Astarte and Ashtaroth and the gods of the nations around them. And the Lord gave them into the hands of Eglon king of Moab, and he ruled over them eighteen years.” This addition links the book to Judges 2:6-13 and 3:12-14.
